The Market Is Watching Itself: Polymarket's Hunt for Insider Bets

Four days before the November 3 midterms, Polymarket is investigating dozens of its own election bets. The platform runs 506 individual election markets, and its compliance team is examining trading that may have used information traders had a duty to protect. At least two cases have already been referred to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The hunt is led by Shana Bautista, a former FBI official who joined Polymarket in June and now runs a 16-person intelligence and investigations team. Its surveillance system pulls gigabytes of data per user — social media, Federal Election Commission filings, banking partners, cryptocurrency records and statistical models — and processes hundreds of alerts a day. Concentrated trading bursts, multiple accounts behaving alike and shared device identifiers all trigger a closer look, and alerts that cross internal thresholds go straight to Bautista's phone.

The money at stake explains the effort. Combined midterm trading across Polymarket and Kalshi passed $220 million by mid-October. Polymarket's House control market has drawn $24 million with Democrats priced at 92%, its Senate market $9 million with Democrats at 66%, and its balance-of-power contracts price a Democratic sweep at 65% against just 8% for a Republican sweep. Texas leads the Senate battlegrounds at $7 million in volume, with Michigan and Maine at $3 million each.

Polymarket is not alone in policing itself. Kalshi banned and fined political candidates for betting on themselves in April and handed a lifetime ban to former Rep. George Santos in July; it has opened more than 150 investigations this year and sent over 20 cases to law enforcement. Polymarket itself had previously referred more than 100 cases across various markets to law enforcement.

That self-policing now carries the market's credibility. Election prices shape fundraising, media narratives and voter perceptions, so a price moved by private polling is not just a bad trade — it distorts the signal everyone else is reading. Bautista's warning is blunt: if you have information you have a duty to protect, do not trade on it — we will find you.

item.title: Washington Sues Back: The CFTC Now Has 10 States in Court — Oct 30, 2026 · 11:10 AM ET
item.description:
Washington Sues Back: The CFTC Now Has 10 States in Court

The prediction market fight is no longer just platforms against states. The federal government sued Utah on Monday, and counting Utah, Washington now has 10 states in court for trying to keep federally regulated exchanges out. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed in federal court in Salt Lake City, less than a week after Utah moved first.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown sued Kalshi and trading firm Susquehanna in state court on October 20, alleging Kalshi has offered gambling bets to residents since at least September 2024 and calling them indistinguishable from what a sportsbook sells. Utah bans gambling outright, and the state seeks to block Kalshi's sports, election and cultural markets and recover the fees it collected. Utah has already beaten Kalshi once: a federal judge ruled for the state in August, and the Tenth Circuit refused emergency relief while Kalshi appeals.

The CFTC's position is that event contracts count as swaps, a category federal commodities law leaves to federal regulators alone, and that letting each state step in would leave exchanges answering to 50 regulators nationwide. Its earlier suits cover Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, New York, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Rhode Island, New Mexico and Kentucky. Judges have sided with Washington so far in Minnesota, Illinois and Arizona, including an October 2 Illinois ruling that the state likely cannot force Kalshi to get a sports wagering license.

Where Washington has not stepped in, the exchanges are suing themselves: Kalshi in Louisiana on October 23, Polymarket US in Louisiana and Ohio, and Nadex and Ludlow in Missouri, whose cease-and-desist letters also remain in play for Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Novig and Underdog.

The appeals courts are split: Nevada won at the Ninth Circuit, the Sixth Circuit turned down Kalshi in Ohio and Tennessee, and New Jersey, which lost at the Third Circuit, has asked the Supreme Court to step in, with Kalshi's reply due November 9. Ten states in court, platforms suing in four more, and a Supreme Court petition pending: this is now a federal fight over who regulates the odds.

item.description:
Election Night Now Has a Ticker: The Odds Move Into the Newsroom

Four days before the November 3 midterms, prediction markets are no longer just a screen traders watch. They are moving into the newsroom itself. CNN, CBS News, CNBC and Dow Jones have entered commercial partnerships with Kalshi and Polymarket to cite election trading odds in their reporting, according to Bloomberg reporting on October 30.

The money explains the attention. Bloomberg analysis of Dune data puts election-related trading volume on Kalshi and Polymarket at about $1.5 billion. Traders are pricing Democrats at 94% to win the House on Polymarket and 69% to take the Senate, with Kalshi close behind at 92.1% for the House and 68.5% for the Senate.

The deals are not all the same. CBS News announced Kalshi as its prediction market sponsor. CNBC disclosed a partnership with Kalshi involving customer acquisition revenue sharing and a minority equity investment. The Wall Street Journal homepage now features a Polymarket odds column.

There are limits, and a debate. Fox and CNN said they will not broadcast odds on air on election night, and some commentators have raised concerns that commercial ties could compromise news independence. That tension is the story: the odds have become too large to ignore, and too commercial to treat as just another poll.

item.description:
Prediction Markets Just Out-Earned Crypto at Robinhood

The crossover is now official — and it is in the earnings. Robinhood reported third-quarter results on October 27, and event contracts generated $173 million in revenue, ahead of the $120 million from cryptocurrency trading, for the second straight quarter.

The volume behind it is enormous. Robinhood customers traded a record 16.4 billion event contracts in the quarter, up from 13.6 billion in the second quarter and more than seven times the year-earlier level. Prediction-market revenue rose 11% quarter over quarter, from $156 million, and more than sixfold year over year, inside record total revenue of $1.42 billion.

The mix is changing, too. Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma said non-sports contracts accounted for roughly 30% of prediction-market activity, up from about 15% in the prior quarter. Rothera, the prediction exchange Robinhood runs with Susquehanna, contributed $28 million and passed $100 million in annualized revenue in its first full quarter.

The exchanges supplying the market set their own records in October. Kalshi posted about $65 billion in volume, 10% above its September record, with open interest at a record $2.05 billion, while Polymarket US reached $10 billion, up roughly 15% from its previous monthly high.

Crypto revenue at Robinhood fell 55% from a year earlier. The forecast, it turns out, is now the bigger business.

item.description:
Bitcoin's $100,000 Question

Two days after the largest crypto theft in history — roughly $6.3 billion drained from Binance in about twenty minutes — the market's biggest question has a brutal answer.

Polymarket prices Bitcoin reaching $100,000 by December 31 at just 12.5%, on $4.0 million traded. Bitcoin spot trades near $77,400 after more than $1 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated in the selloff, and Ethereum has slid to two-month lows near $2,178.

The hack changed the math. Roughly $3 billion in stolen stablecoins has been frozen by Tether, Circle and others — but an estimated $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum sits beyond reach in dormant wallets that traders will watch for years.

Not long ago, $100,000 by Christmas looked conservative. Today the market says one in eight. That gap — between the narrative and the number — is exactly what prediction markets exist to measure.

item.description:
One Exchange, Fifty Fights: The States vs. Kalshi

Kalshi raised $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation on Thursday. It is also, at the same time, fighting for its legal life in courtrooms across America.

Utah has filed 14 criminal charges against Kalshi's co-founders. The CFTC has sued Utah right back, calling the charges federal overreach, and the CFTC's enforcement chief has named insider trading a top prediction-market priority.

The courts cannot agree with each other. State regulators have prevailed in Nevada, Maryland and Ohio — the Sixth Circuit recently ruled against Kalshi's federal preemption argument — while Kalshi won relief in Tennessee. Eleven states are pursuing legal action in total.

The market is adapting in real time. When Phantom rolled Kalshi markets into its wallet app this month, it blocked sports contracts in Michigan, and sports, elections and politics in Nevada and Washington.

There is now a market on whether the Supreme Court accepts a sports event contract case by December 31 — priced at 23.5%. The industry's future may be decided there.

item.description: - **ConnectSafely publishes a parent guide to Kalshi warning that the platform is not for minors and that CFTC regulation does not make trading risk-free, ConnectSafely reports** — The guide says Kalshi requires users to be at least 18 and uses identity verification, and that participants can lose money when a prediction is wrong.
